Guardrails
—
The halo means presence, not progress. It never fills, never counts down, never implies a percentage.
—
Running is blue to ice. Needs you is cyan and quieter. Keeping the hues apart is what stops the two signals blurring into one glow.
—
Needs you keeps its own weight: the tidepool dot, the accent rule, and a named action. The halo is added on top, never in place of them.
—
Queued, stuck, and done are matte. A halo on a card nobody is working on is decoration.

Under reduced motion the halo holds at its mid-breath frame. The signal survives, the movement stops.

Later
Hold anywhere to answer
The orb is the instrument
No talk dock. Voice lives on the orb the way ElevenLabs puts it there: volume moves the petals inside the sphere, and the Undertow stays outside it. Two signals, one object — audio in the body, work state in the aura.
Standing
Awake, no audio. Two pale lobes barely moving.
You, holding
Input volume drives the petals. Blue, wide, agitated.
Walkie, talking
Output volume. Ice and cyan, slower and rounder.
Running
No audio at all. Petals settle, the Undertow does the talking.
Needs you
Quiet cyan ring, petals almost gone. It is waiting, not working.
The talk dock carried three jobs. The orb and the gesture absorb all three, and the screen gets 152px back.
The button
A 358px capsule you had to reach for. Now the whole stage is the button — hold anywhere, and one mist-grey line says so.
was: capsule · now: gesture
The waveform
Thirty-two bars in a pill, duplicated on every screen. Now input volume moves the petals inside the sphere you are already looking at.
was: 32 bars · now: petals
Send and cancel
Two more targets. Now release sends, slide up cancels, and neither needs a control drawn on screen.
was: 2 targets · now: 0
Two clocks on one object
—
Petals run on the audio clock — per frame, driven by input or output volume. They are allowed to be jumpy because speech is.
—
The Undertow runs on the work clock — 3.4s to 9s, outside the sphere. It never reacts to sound, so voice and work never fight for the same edge.
—
Blue petals are you. Ice and cyan petals are walkie. If both are silent the sphere is nearly white, whatever the session is doing.
—
When you talk over a running session both show at once — blue inside, blue-to-cyan aura outside. That overlap is the point, not a collision.
What the transport puts on screen
OpenAI Realtime over WebRTC is not a detail behind the orb. The handshake has four steps and a visible cost, turn-taking has a default the walkie gesture argues with, and two of its hardest properties are invisible at runtime — which makes them a UI problem, not a backend one.
The ring around the orb is the handshake, not a spinner. Four real steps, four segments, and the ring is gone the moment the session is live.
01
Secret
The service calls POST /v1/realtime/client_secrets with the API key. TTL 10 to 7200s, default 600 — and it governs session creation only.
02
SDP
The client does the exchange itself. Raw body, Content-Type application/sdp, bearer of the ephemeral key. Not the multipart form.
03
Call id
The answer is raw SDP; the id arrives in the Location header as /v1/realtime/calls/rtc_… Only the client sees it, so relaying it is required.
04
Sideband
The service opens wss://…/v1/realtime?call_id=… with the standard key. This is where tools get answered.
05
session.created
Live. The ring dissolves and the elapsed clock starts here — it is the only clock the API gives you.
The fork worth deciding before any of this gets built. WebRTC keeps audio flowing over the media track the whole time, so these are not two settings — they are two different pieces of choreography, and only one of them is the default.
Server VAD
default
turn_detection: on
mic stays open for the whole call
the model decides when you stopped
it answers on its own judgement of the pause
An always-open mic needs a mute control you can hit without looking, and a long pause mid-thought gets read as a finished turn.
→ Orb up · open mic
Push to talk
opt-in
turn_detection: null
input_audio_buffer.clear on press
commit then response.create on release
output_audio_buffer.clear to barge in
The mic is only live while you hold, which is the walkie gesture and the better privacy story — but the buffer choreography is yours, and assuming it matches the WebSocket flow ships a broken button.
→ Orb up · you talking
Two properties of the API that never announce themselves. Both become interface problems, because the only place they can be handled is before the user notices.
The 60-minute cap has no event
No expiry event, no warning, no disconnect reason. The client tracks elapsed time from session.created and re-establishes before the cap, re-seeding from Postgres. On screen it has to read as continuity, not as an error — nothing red, nothing to acknowledge.
→ Orb up · re-established
Truncation is silent and lossy
When the window fills, the oldest messages are dropped with no summarization and no error, so the model can stay fluent about a question that is no longer there. The interface can never present the conversation as the record — asks and receipts are read from the store.
→ Orb down · undertow
A runtime with a session at the centre
The architecture doc rejected an agent as the router. It did not reject an agent in the system — it rejected one in the critical path holding state. Put the orchestrator beside the fast path instead of inside it and every objection either retires or is answerable, while the thing you actually want — judgement, orchestration, and somewhere to think — becomes possible.
Not three layers stacked — three planes that answer in parallel. Any one of them can be busy or dead without silencing the others.

owns

answers in
under two seconds, always
woken by
the call itself
never
thinks, decides, or holds an opinion
Judgement
owns
triage, moving work between sessions, and the conversation you are having
answers in
seconds to minutes — and that is allowed
woken by
you, /loop, or /schedule
never
holds the only copy of anything
Direct
owns
one worker session, by voice or by chat, with nothing in between
answers in
whatever that session takes
woken by

never
routes, orchestrates, or speaks for another session
What this does to the decided architecture. Two of the three arguments that killed the agent-router are still binding — they are not refuted here, they are contained. The containment is the design.
retired
“The router was justified by the belief that switching a realtime session between workspaces is hard. That belief is false — it is one session.update.”
The orchestrator is not there to route. Workspace switching stays a session.update on the fast path. Its justification is judgement, which is a different claim and has to carry itself.
still binding
“A single Claude session serializes every workspace behind one turn chain, so an urgent ask queues behind a ten-minute turn.”
Contained by never putting it on the critical path. What is blocked, read me the last turn, and every ask answer are served from Postgres in under two seconds. The moment the orchestrator is what answers those, this argument kills the design a second time.
still binding
“Compaction silently destroys ticket-to-workspace bindings, producing readbacks that are fluent, confident and about the wrong repository.”
Contained by giving it nothing authoritative to lose. Bindings live in the store; the orchestrator reads them like any other client; the thread is a projection, never the record. It is free to compact.
extends
“An ask is structured data — never free text. The service must be structurally unable to originate a workspace call from a worker-supplied string.”
Extended to the orchestrator. It cannot post free text into a session either: a dispatch is a typed proposal, checked against the host allowlist, shown on screen, and sent only when you say so.
gained
“Voice replaces a reviewable, logged, textual approval with an ephemeral acoustic one, and leaves no audit artifact.”
Weakened, on purpose. Every spoken exchange writes to the thread, so discussion becomes reviewable after the fact. That is what lets walkie widen from triage into thinking. It does not make voice authoritative — earshot is still authentication, and consequential approval still happens on a screen.
The same orb at four altitudes. What surrounds it says who you are talking to, so a request can never be aimed at the wrong level by accident — and the chrome follows: workspace chips appear at session altitude, orbiting sessions replace them at orchestrator altitude.
Turn
one thing an agent just did
“read me the last turn on seaslug”
nothing — the orb is only a speaker
Session
one workspace, directly
“seaslug, skip the flaky spec and keep going”
workspace chips
Orchestrator
across sessions, with judgement
“is anything actually waiting on me?”
the sessions it governs, orbiting
Standing
work that wakes itself — /loop and /schedule
“every morning, tell me what broke overnight”
a quiet ring and one waking mark
Two modes, and the thread underneath both
Altitude says who you are addressing. Mode says what kind of exchange it is — and the two have different latency contracts, different sources of truth, and different things left behind. Showing which one you are in is what keeps a two-second fact from being mistaken for an opinion.
Triage
ANSWERED BY
the Reflex plane, reading Postgres
LATENCY
under two seconds, whatever the orchestrator is doing
LEAVES BEHIND
a receipt line — the query, and how long it took
WHY YOU CAN TRUST IT
it never passed through a model's memory, so it cannot be fluently wrong about which repository
Think
ANSWERED BY
the orchestrator session, in its own words
LATENCY
seconds to minutes, and the orb says so
LEAVES BEHIND
the thread — which is the audit artifact voice was missing
THE STANDING RULE
nothing said in it reaches a session until a typed dispatch is shown and confirmed
When the voice is poor
Poor in both senses, and they land in the same place. Bad audio drops you into the thread with the exchange intact. A request voice is simply bad at — anything with a diff, a list, a blast radius — drops you into the same thread, same addressee, mid-conversation. The thread is not a degraded mode. It is the record the call is writing the whole time, and it is always one tap away.
Aligned to Maestro
The design system already decided several things walkie was deciding again, and contradicted a few choices outright. Where Maestro is explicit, Maestro wins — walkie is a phone client for the same work model, not a separate product.
Corrected
“Running state wears the Undertow, not a colored border.”
The coloured left rule came off all sixteen rows across the document. The halo carries running on its own, which is what it was for.
“Needing you is a gate, not a failure — mark halts in accent-blue, never red.”
The consequential ask went from amber to tidepool. Amber is now reserved for a genuine fault — degraded audio — and never for something waiting on you.
“The branch is the receipt. Never fake progress percentages.”
Evidence rows carry run/mut-8821, the diffstat, and the judge verdict instead of prose. The lifecycle rail is five named stages, not a bar that fills.
“The look is the transaction — what changed · what it decided · what it asks.”
Built as App · The look. It was the primitive walkie was missing, and it is also exactly the shape a voice readback needs, which is why walkie can speak it.
Already aligned
“Chat is a projection. A session renders the work; it never owns it.”
Arrived at independently last turn, from the truncation constraint. Same conclusion, different route: the thread is a projection of the store, never the record.
“The orchestrator is an agent — presence in the chrome, a session you can open, a wake log. Never a settings page.”
The Judgement plane, addressable from the switcher, with Standing on Home. No settings screen anywhere in the app.
“Calm is load-bearing. Live signals breathe, they don't spin for attention.”
The Undertow breathes. The connect ring is four discrete handshake steps, not a spinner — it reports position in a real sequence.
“The gate is yours. No loop can auto-Done. Approving is the one human verb.”
Approve and Send back are the only controls on the look, and anything irreversible leaves the call for a screen.
Still divergent
“Tight scale: 12 / 14 / 16 / 18 / 22 / 24 / 28. Nothing else.”
walkie.pen runs 11 / 13 / 15 / 17 throughout and pre-dates this work. Aligning it is a document-wide sweep and a decision, not a tidy-up. Flagged, not done.
“Setting a schedule is a sentence.”
Standing routines show on Home with the cause of their last wake, but there is no surface where you create one by saying it. Not built.
“Glass appears in exactly three places: overlays, popovers, the composer.”
walkie uses it for the orb dock and the push notification. Both are defensible — the dock is the composer — but the dramatic halo should be the dock's alone, and it currently is not.
Understop — the current, arrested
Not a quieter Undertow — its sibling. Same water, same material, but the flow has stopped: the orbit holds at its last angle, the tide flattens into a level line, and the pools settle either side of it. Water in motion has weather. Water at rest has a surface. That difference is the whole signal.

At orb scale there is room for all three layers, so the difference is unmistakable: the Undertow's arc sweeps and its tide rises on the diagonal; the Understop holds one arc where it stopped and lays the tide flat across the middle.
Undertow · running
Understop · paused
At dot scale the same rule holds. The tidepool dot drifts on a diagonal because the weather is moving through it. The meniscus dot holds a level line, because the water has found its surface and stopped.

What moves, and how little
ORBIT
Stopped. It holds the angle it stopped at, at half opacity — the current's last known position. The Undertow's turns continuously over 9s.
TIDE
No travel. A level line with about one percent of surface tension over 6s. The Undertow's band rises counter-phase over 3.4s.
POOLS
12s, four percent amplitude. Settled, not dead — the difference between a paused run and a finished one.
REDUCED MOTION
Unchanged. It is already almost still, which is the point: the accessible frame and the intended frame are the same picture.
COLOUR
Tidepool cyan and ice, never the running blue. Hue does the work at a glance; the geometry confirms it on a second look.
The rule that keeps them apart
One signal family, two states of the same water. The Undertow is motion with no destination — presence, never progress. The Understop is that motion held: the flow reached something it cannot pass without you.
Only work that was running can wear the Understop. A queued item never moved, so it gets nothing; a done item released the halo. This is what stops it becoming a decoration for anything mildly important.
The two never appear on the same surface at the same intensity. On Home the running group breathes and the halted card holds still, so a glance from across the room separates them before a single word is read.
Both retire the moment their cause does. The Understop clears when you answer — not when the run resumes, because the run resuming is the consequence, not the event.

The same two signals, as shaders

What the shaders buy, and what they cost
THEY ACTUALLY MOVE
Every halo above this board is one frame of a three-rhythm animation, chosen by hand. These run — 4.2s against 3.4s against 9s, which is what stops the Undertow ever quite repeating. That property cannot be drawn.
THE SDF FINDS THE SHAPE
@sdf gives the halo the outline of whatever it wraps, so one file serves a row, a card, a group and a circle. The gradient version needed the stops re-tuned for every aspect ratio, and did the corners badly.
THE UNIFORMS ARE THE RUNTIME
u_volume is getInputVolume. u_held is the angle the orbit stopped at. u_level is where the waterline sits. These are not styling knobs — they are the state, which means design and implementation stop drifting apart.
ONE FILE PER SIGNAL
undertow.glsl and understop.glsl are the whole specification, and they are the artefact that ships. No token set to keep in sync, no per-scale variants.
THE COST · REDUCED MOTION
A CSS keyframe stops with prefers-reduced-motion for free. A shader must be told: freeze u_time at the mid-breath frame. Understop is nearly there already; Undertow needs the branch written.
THE COST · IT IS A GPU SURFACE
Text over it stays DOM, so contrast and selection are unaffected — but every haloed row is a live WebGL context on a phone. On a list of eight running sessions that is a battery decision, not an aesthetic one. Cap the count, or render one shared layer behind the group.
The orb, rethought as a point cloud
A lattice of points on a sphere, monochrome, shaded by depth. It reads as an instrument rather than a lava lamp — and it hands the whole colour axis back to the work signal, so the orb says what the agent is doing while the halo around it says what the work is doing.

What this buys: the orb and the halo stop competing
THE ORB IS MONOCHROME
It carries what the agent is doing right now — listening, speaking, thinking, connecting — as motion of a point lattice. No hue at all, which is what the design system asks for and what my petal version was quietly spending.
THE HALO KEEPS THE COLOUR
Undertow and Understop stay on the blue axis around it. So one object answers two different questions at once without either signal borrowing the other's vocabulary.
ONE DARK OBJECT IN A LIGHT APP
A point cloud is luminous, which needs a dark ground. That makes the orb the single dark thing on a white screen — which is what the Broomva blackhole mark already is. The comparison row above has it on paper, on ink, and on deep blue so the ground can be chosen rather than assumed.
THE STATES ARE UNIFORMS, NOT ARTWORK
standing is spin 0.16 and nothing else. you-talking is u_volume, which drives dot size and brightness rather than deforming the sphere — louder reads as a brighter lattice. walkie-talking is u_wave, a band travelling up. thinking is spin plus a little scatter. connecting is scatter resolving to zero.
KNOWN, UNRESOLVED
Two things are not settled. u_scatter — the dissolve used for connecting — reliably blanks the sphere in this renderer at any non-zero value, so connecting is expressed with u_radius instead and the dissolve is parked. And at 44px in the dock a 170-point lattice will very likely turn to mush; the reference ships a 20px variant, so it is solvable, but it is a fork in the shader rather than a scale factor.
One object: the voices inside, the work outside
The lattice and the halo are now the same shader, so they composite instead of stacking. Inside the sphere, two voices with two different gestures — yours lifts the whole lattice, walkie's lifts only the band it is travelling through. Outside it, the Undertow when work is running and the Understop when it has stopped on you.

What each uniform is wired to
u_in ← getInputVolume()
Your voice lifts the whole lattice at once — every point brighter and slightly larger, tinted toward blue. It is an undirected gesture because your speech arrives all at once from outside the sphere.
u_out ← getOutputVolume()
Walkie's voice lifts only the band it is travelling through, rising up the sphere on a 2.5s cycle and tinting it ice. Directed, because its speech is being produced from somewhere.
BOTH AT ONCE
Full duplex is now a single picture rather than two states: a blue lattice with an ice band moving through it. That is the barge-in case, and it is the one thing the previous two-state orb could not say.
u_work ← the run
The Undertow, outside the sphere. Pools on 4.2s, tide on 3.4s, orbit on 9s, never quite repeating. It does not react to sound at all, so voice and work never fight for the same edge.
u_paused ← the ask
The Understop replaces it: the tide finds its level and lays a line straight through, the orbit holds where it stopped. Visible in the last case, and unmistakable next to a running one.
THE DIVISION HOLDS
Inside the sphere is who is speaking. Outside it is what the work is doing. One object, two questions, and neither borrows the other's vocabulary — which is what the separate halo and orb could never quite guarantee.
Two things were wrong, and one of them was not taste
THE WHITE SMUDGE WAS A BUG
The compositing chain already produces premultiplied colour — halo over body over lattice — and then the shader multiplied by alpha a second time. Every soft region got washed toward the background, which is the pale haze that sat between the dots and the blue. One line.
THE LATTICE HAS A NATURAL SIZE
It reads as texture at roughly 44 to 96 pixels and as a grid of polka dots much above that, whatever the dot size or count. The reference ships 20px and 64px for the same reason. Raising the count to 340 or 520 to compensate hangs the renderer, so that escape is closed.
SO SCALE COMES FROM THE WEATHER
u_radius 0.26 rather than 0.52: the sphere stays around fifty pixels and the halo takes the rest of the frame. The hero orb is now large because the Undertow is large, not because the lattice was stretched — which is the right hierarchy anyway, since the weather is the part that carries across a room.
STILL OPEN
At dock size the sphere would be about twelve pixels at this ratio, which is too small to read. Small placements likely want u_radius back near 0.5 with the halo suppressed — one more uniform pairing to settle, not a new shader.
The lattice and the weather do not scale together, so the component needs presets rather than one set of numbers. Shown at true size, because legibility at size is the entire question.
dock · 44px
Radius 0.66, no halo. There is no room for weather at this size, so the run state is carried by the row it sits in — not by the orb.
inline · 88px
Radius 0.46. Enough ring for the Undertow to register as a tint without the lattice thinning out.
hero · 200px
Radius 0.26. The sphere holds near fifty pixels and the weather takes the rest of the frame.
What if the weather does not stop at the surface. The pools become volumes drifting through the sphere and the tide a plane sweeping it, so points light up as the run passes through them. Work moves in three dimensions, voice moves on the surface — which is what keeps them apart now that they share the same space.
running · contained
The rule as built: weather outside, lattice inside.
running · bleeding
The run passes through the sphere. Points take the blue as a pool crosses them.
paused · bleeding
Same weather as the run, in the cyan palette. Nothing about the motion changes.
you, over a bleeding run
Both at once. Your voice lifts every point; the run only tints the ones it is inside.
Letting the weather inside, and what it costs
IT IS THE TRUER STATEMENT
The run is happening inside the machine, not around it. A ring says the work is adjacent to the agent; a pool crossing the lattice says the agent is the thing doing it. Same information, a better sentence.
IT FORCED A CLEANER SPLIT
Sharing one space meant voice and work could not both own hue — your blue and the run's blue were the same mark, and the fourth case proved it. So voice is now size and brightness, work is colour. That rule is better than the one it replaced and it only surfaced because of this question.
THE UNDERSTOP GAINS THE MOST
The waterline stops being a line drawn beside the orb and becomes one plane passing through it, so the inside and the outside are the same plane. On paper especially it now reads as a single continuous object rather than a sphere with a mark near it.
WHAT IT COSTS
The sphere is no longer neutral. With a run bleeding and a voice lifting at the same time the lattice is genuinely busy, and a third simultaneous signal would break it. Whatever comes next has to go outside, or not exist.
SMALL SIZES KEEP THE OLD RULE
At dock size the internal weather is a handful of pixels and reads as noise. Below roughly 88px, u_bleed goes to zero and the contained version stands — which the size presets above already assume.
MY CALL
Default it on above 88px. It is semantically better, it improved the channel split, and it is the first version where the orb and the halo look like one object instead of two layers that happen to be concentric.
Three attempts at paused, and why the good-looking one was wrong
THE HELD ARC HAD TO GO
A stopped orbit sounds right and looks like a smear — a diagonal streak leaking off one side that read as a rendering fault, not as stillness. Stillness is better carried by everything else going quiet than by freezing one moving part.
THE FILL LOOKED BEST AND SAID THE WRONG THING
Filling the sphere to a level gave it real mass and was easily the most attractive version. It also draws a half-full vessel, which reads as a progress meter — the one thing this system refuses to show. Dropped on those grounds, not on looks.
A LATTICE CANNOT DRAW A LINE
Asking the points to describe the level produced a scatter of cyan dots, because a lattice only has ink where points happen to fall. The surface is now drawn as one continuous mark across the sphere, and the points near it merely tint. That is the version on the board.
WHAT PAUSED IS NOW
The lattice hushes to about sixty percent, one level crosses it, and the same level continues softly outside as a wide low band. No motion, no fill, no frozen arc — a surface at rest, which is what the state actually is.
The same orb on paper
Not an inversion. On a dark ground the lattice is luminous and the sphere needs no form — the points make it. On paper that is gone, so the body is dropped entirely: the page becomes the sphere and the lattice alone describes its surface. Same shader, five uniforms different.

What actually changes between the two modes
u_body 1 → 0
The one real decision. On a dark ground the sphere needs a body to contain the light. On paper the body is what ruins it — a filled disc with even dots reads as a golf ball. Drop it and the page becomes the sphere; the lattice alone describes the surface, and the rim crowding does the rest.
u_shade 0 → 1
Only matters when a body is present. It gives the sphere a lit side, a shaded side and a hairline, and it steepens the depth falloff so the far side genuinely recedes instead of showing through.
INK, NOT BLACK
Dots are #2A3140, not the full ink. At full strength on near-white the lattice is harsh and mechanical; a step lighter and it reads as graphite pressed into the page.
WALKIE GOES TIDEPOOL
Ice reads on a dark sphere and vanishes on paper, so walkie's voice tints to tidepool in light mode. Yours stays blue in both. Two hues that survive both grounds, which is the constraint that picked them.
THE HALO IS MASKED
Without a body there is nothing to stop the Undertow flooding through the middle of the lattice, so the weather is now explicitly kept outside the sphere radius. Harmless in dark mode, load-bearing in light.
WHAT DID NOT CHANGE
Every state, every rhythm, and both voice gestures. One file serves both grounds on five uniforms — no second shader, no forked artwork.
The one open choice in light mode. Without a body there is nothing to stop the weather glowing through the middle of the lattice; with one, the occlusion is clean but the constellation becomes an object again. Both at hero size, same uniforms otherwise.
bodiless
The page is the sphere. Lighter, and it belongs to a paper app — but the halo sits behind the points rather than around them, and the glow leaks into the middle.
near-white body
Clean occlusion and a real silhouette. Heavier: it reads as an object placed on the page rather than drawn into it, and the sphere edge competes with the halo.
My call: bodiless. At hero size the body brings the golf-ball read straight back, and the glow that leaks through is semantically right anyway — the work surrounds the agent, it is not hidden behind it. Keep the body for anywhere the orb sits on a busy or coloured surface, where occlusion stops being optional.
The same bleed in light mode. On paper it is arguably clearer: the ink lattice is neutral, so a pool crossing it reads as colour arriving in a specific part of the sphere rather than a general glow.
running · bleeding
paused · bleeding
you, over a run
Paused, as the same weather in another palette
Every attempt to give paused its own geometry failed — a held arc read as a rendering fault, a fill read as a progress meter, a drawn level read as a slice. So the motion is now identical to the Undertow and only the palette changes. Same pools, same tide, same orbit; the run reference sits first for comparison.

Verdict: tidepool, and running gives up cyan
TIDEPOOL → CYAN
The system already gives cyan to Needs you, and it separates from the run's blue at a glance in both modes. Cyan to white is brighter and reads slightly hot for a state that is a gate rather than a failure — worth keeping as the variant for anywhere the orb has to compete with a busy surface.
DRAINED WAS THE INTERESTING FAILURE
Desaturating the run to a grey-blue is the obvious way to say stopped, and it says the wrong stopped: it reads as inactive, finished, switched off. Paused is not dormant — something is waiting on you, and the colour has to keep some pressure.
INVERTED WAS TOO CLOSE
Navy with a cyan highlight is legible on its own and nearly indistinguishable from the run in peripheral vision, which is the only vision that matters for an ambient signal.
THE REAL FIX WAS ON THE OTHER SIDE
Separation was muddy until running stopped using cyan. On paper its highlight had been tidepool, so the two states were competing for one hue. Running is now blue only — blue to ice in dark, blue to blue-ink on paper — and cyan belongs to paused alone.
WHAT THIS COSTS
In light mode walkie's voice tint moves from cyan to blue-ink, so the two voices are closer in hue there. Acceptable, because voice is carried by size and brightness while work owns colour — but it does mean hue can no longer be used to tell you from walkie on paper.
The app
Fifty screens, one spine, both themes. A native Swift client on your own tailnet, talking to Genesis on the host beside the sessions. The orb is present on every surface — collapsed in the dock or filling the stage — and answers two questions at once: the lattice inside says who is speaking, the weather outside says what the work is doing. Everything else is navigation between three places, plus the rooms you visit once.
The spine
HOME ⇄ VOICE ⇄ THREAD
Home is the bench: what wants you, what is running, what is standing. Pull the orb up and you are in Voice at whatever altitude the chip says. One tap from Voice is the Thread, which is the record the call has been writing the whole time. Those three cover the entire ordinary day; everything else is entered from them or from a push.
THE GESTURES
Hold anywhere on the stage to talk · release to send · slide up to cancel · tap the chip to change who you are addressing · pull the dock up to open the call · tap Show thread to drop out of voice without losing the exchange · swipe down to collapse back to the bench.
Entry points
COLD START — Pair → Microphone → Home
Two products, once: Tailscale, then the host command. walkie cannot join a tailnet on its own, so first run is a two-step and the second step only lights up when the first has. The allowlist starts empty on purpose. Microphone asks once and says plainly that hold-to-talk keeps the mic closed between turns.
A PUSH — Push → Ask
The only path that skips the bench. The notification states the options count, that evidence is attached, and that voice will not answer this one. It deep-links to Ask, never into a call.
A ROUTINE — Standing → Routine
Set by saying it, never by a form. The list shows why each one last woke; the detail is a wake log, not a settings page.
What each screen is for
ENTRY · row 1
Pair (Tailscale, then the host) · Microphone · Connecting (four real steps, not a spinner) · Host offline (you are on the tailnet, Genesis is not answering) · Off tailnet (the host may be fine — this is the phone's side) · Empty (nothing reachable yet)
BENCH · row 2
Home (needs you, running, standing) · Home all quiet (the good day) · Switcher (who you are addressing, and what that costs) · Standing (routines and their last wake) · Routine (the wake log)
VOICE · rows 3 and 4
orchestrator (thinking with you) · store answered (a fact, 41ms, nothing woken) · escalated (judgement engaged, the sessions gather) · session idle (one altitude down) · you talking · walkie talking · barge-in (both at once) · degraded (audio poor, call intact) · re-established (the 60-minute cap, handled early)
WORK · row 5
Session (one workspace) · Look contained (voice may approve, containment proven) · Look needs a screen (voice may only open it) · Look approved · Look sent back · Ask low stakes (the everyday one, answerable out loud) · Ask consequential (the deep link, evidence in mono, no wave capsule) · Ask answered (with an undo window) · Receipts (rung three, opt-in)
THREADS AND SYSTEM
Thread orchestrator (with a typed dispatch proposal) · Thread seaslug (direct, with tool receipts) · Dispatch sent · Push · Access (the allowlist, and what voice can never do)
The rules the screens are obeying
Running wears the Undertow, paused wears the same weather in cyan, and nothing else moves. Colour belongs to work; size and brightness belong to voice. Needing you is a gate, not a failure — it is never red. Approving is the one human verb, and it happens by voice only where containment is machine-proven. The thread is the audit artifact that voice was missing, which is what lets walkie be used for thinking and not only for triage.
Where it runs
Phone and host meet on the tailnet; both reach OpenAI over the internet independently. There is no cloud half — a host-resident Genesis satisfies same-UID trust by construction, which is the only thing the old split existed to arrange. The costs are named on the topology board: the host becomes a single point, onboarding gains a dependency, and off-tailnet is a failure mode that needs its own words because the remedy is on the phone rather than the workstation.
Turn-taking, decided
Hold to talk is the default. The product is named after the gesture, the mic stays closed between turns, and earshot being the authentication boundary is a much smaller surface when the mic is shut. Open mic remains available per session — wiring WebRTC directly rather than adopting PushToTalk kept full duplex, so this is a preference rather than a one-way door. Barge-in works in both: under the default you press to cut in, and the overlap while walkie's audio ducks out is real rather than a hard switch, which is why the orb shows both voices during it.
Both themes, from one set of screens
Nothing is drawn twice. Every screen and every shared component points at themed tokens, so switching the mode axis repaints all thirty-four. The orb goes with them: u_sphere, u_ink, u_agent, u_body and u_shade are variables rather than constants, which means the sphere inverts on its own — bodiless ink on paper, a filled luminous lattice on dark. The one rule that survives both is the size split: below 88px the orb keeps a body in either theme, because a bodiless constellation at dock scale is dust.
The rooms you visit once
ONBOARDING
welcome · scope explainer (what voice will and will not do, said before you rely on it) · pair · microphone · microphone denied · notifications · add workspace · ready
SETTINGS
settings root · turn-taking (the decided fork, exposed) · voice and readback · notifications · appearance (theme, reduced motion, orb density) · diagnostics (link, this call, store, build)
INSTANCES
workspaces · workspace detail · orchestrator scope · history
THE ONE ABSENCE
There is no page for the orchestrator's instructions, personality or schedule. It is an agent, not a preference: what it should do is something you tell it, and the wake log shows what it did. Its scope screen exists because reachability is a security surface — the rest would be a settings page for something that should have been told.
How far the signal reduces
A Live Activity cannot run a shader — it is a constrained view on a slow update budget. So before drawing any ambient surface, the question is how small the Undertow can get and still say running rather than decorative. It survives three steps down and then becomes a different mark entirely.
200px · stage
Lattice, weather, both voices. Everything.
88px · inline
Lattice thins but the weather still reads.
44px · dock
Needs a body. Texture, not points.
15px · dot
Not a sphere any more. One drifting gradient.
At dot scale the design system already had the answer: the tidepool dot is the same weather at 15px. Paused takes the level, which survives at this size because it is one straight edge rather than a shape.

What the ambient layer does to the app we built
THE DOT IS THE REDUCTION, NOT A SMALLER ORB
Below about 44px the lattice stops being a sphere and becomes noise, so the ambient surfaces do not shrink the orb — they switch to the tidepool dot the design system already specified. Running drifts on the diagonal, needs-you holds one level edge. Both survive at 13px on a black pill, which is the hardest test in the set.
THE ORB SURVIVES IN EXACTLY ONE AMBIENT PLACE
The expanded Island, at 44px with a body. Everywhere smaller it is a dot; everywhere larger you are already in the app. That is a clean rule and it means only one extra asset.
HOME LOSES ITS JOB, NOT ITS LAYOUT
Running and needs-you now live on the Lock Screen and the widget. What is left that is only in the app is Standing, Done, and the threads. Home all quiet is the clearest casualty — the good day is the day the widget is enough and nothing opens.
PUSH BECOMES A LIVE ACTIVITY
The banner was the web's ceiling. A Live Activity persists, updates, and carries a real button. The consequential ask still refuses to be answerable from it — Answer opens the screen with the evidence, exactly as before.
ONE PROMISE NEEDS REWRITING
App · Microphone says the mic is live only while your thumb is down. Under PushToTalk there is a joined-channel state and a system indicator that this sentence does not describe. That copy is wrong the moment Swift is the direction.
WHAT DOES NOT MOVE
Every screen in row five. Session, both Looks, Ask, Receipts and Access are the deliberate opposite of ambient — they exist because something needed your eyes on a screen with the evidence in front of you. No amount of native surface changes that, and if it ever seems to, that is the security argument eroding rather than the design improving.
Three legs, one tailnet
The phone is native Swift and joins the tailnet. Genesis runs on the host beside the sessions it reaches. There is no cloud half any more — the thing that made the deployment split structural was a Railway container being unable to satisfy same-UID trust, and a host-resident service satisfies it by construction.
THE LEGS
phone ⇄ host · over Tailscale
Everything that is walkie's own traffic. A WebSocket at /ws carries session state and turn events; the ask log, the ephemeral-secret request, the call-id relay and typed dispatches ride the same Hono surface. Nothing is exposed inbound — the tailnet is the authentication boundary, which is a stronger statement than the bearer check it replaces.
phone ⇄ OpenAI · over the internet
The WebRTC media path only. The client still does its own SDP exchange with the ephemeral key, exactly as before. This leg does not touch the tailnet and does not need the host to be reachable once it is up.
host ⇄ OpenAI · over the internet
The sideband, with the standard API key, plus the tool calls Genesis answers. Same as the decided design; it simply lives on the workstation now instead of in Railway.
host → APNs → phone
Push is outbound from the host, so it works without any inbound exposure and without a cloud relay. It is also the one leg that does not care whether the phone is on the tailnet.
WHAT THIS RETIRES
The cloud half, and with it the fan-out service, the artifact server, and the outbound-only Tailscale hop from host to Railway. The doc calls treating these as one deployable “the mistake that makes the whole thing undeployable” — that was true of a Railway container. It is not true of a host-resident Genesis, and the paragraph needs rewriting rather than reinterpreting.
WHAT IT COSTS
The host becomes the single point. With a cloud half, an ask could be queued and pushed while the workstation slept; now a sleeping host means no asks reach you at all. That is a real availability regression and it should be a stated product decision, not a discovery.
Onboarding gains a dependency. The phone cannot silently join a tailnet — Tailscale is a separate app the user installs and signs into before walkie can reach anything. First run is now two products, not one.
A new failure mode that is not host-offline. Off-tailnet means the host may be perfectly healthy and simply unreachable; the remedy is on the phone, not the workstation, so it needs its own screen and its own words.
WHAT IT IMPROVES
Same-UID trust stops being a design problem and becomes a property of where the code runs. The unix socket under /tmp/cc-socks/ is reachable because Genesis is on the same machine as the sessions, which is what the whole host-agent indirection existed to arrange.
Full duplex stays available. Wiring WebRTC directly with a plain audio session — rather than adopting the PushToTalk framework — keeps both turn-taking modes on the table, so the open-mic question stays open instead of being foreclosed by the client choice.
What Genesis actually provides
Read out of apps/genesis rather than assumed. Where the design invented a name, this is the name. Where walkie adds a concept Genesis does not have, that is stated as ours to build rather than left looking like something we can call.
THE PHASE MACHINE — packages/projection/src/reducer.ts
RunPhase = "idle" | "running" | "awaiting" | "blocked" | "done"
walkie's plain-voice states map onto it, but not one to one. Running is running. Needs you is awaiting. Stuck is blocked. Done is done. Queued has no Genesis phase — idle is a thread that has never run, which is not the same thing. Standing has none at all: a routine is walkie's, and nothing in the reducer knows about cadence.
The important one: awaiting is entered when the agent calls AskUserQuestion, and the reducer captures pendingQuestion off that tool call. So a walkie ask is not a message we parse — it is a tool invocation with a schema, and its named options are the tool's options. The claim that an ask is structured data and never free text is therefore already true in the engine, not a rule walkie has to impose.
done and blocked are absorbing. awaiting survives a turn-ending result, which is why a run can sit waiting on you with no process running.
THE SURFACE — apps/api/src/server.ts, Hono
GET /workspaces · POST /workspaces · DELETE /workspaces/:id · GET /workspaces/available · GET /workspaces/browse · POST /workspaces/refresh
GET /workspaces/:id/git/status · /git/diff · POST /git/commit · GET /workspaces/:id/checks · /files · /file
GET /threads · GET /threads/:id · POST /message · POST /control · GET /health
POST /control takes an action of reset · interrupt · status · archive · unarchive · rename. walkie's Interrupt is that interrupt. walkie's Send back is a POST /message on the thread. walkie's Approve has no counterpart — there is no gate in Genesis, so the gate is ours to define and ours to enforce.
TRANSPORT — corrected
It is a WebSocket at /ws?thread=<id>, not SSE. The topology board said SSE for the ask log and session state; that was assumed and is now fixed. Genesis upgrades with createBunWebSocket and the PWA connects per thread — walkie either does the same or adds a fan-out of its own, but it cannot describe what exists today as SSE.
THE WORKSPACE RECORD — packages/core/src/types.ts
Workspace { id, name, rootPath, isGitRepo?, noWorktree?, confined?, home? }
Session { id, workspaceId, threadId, agentSessionId?, phase, engine?, noWorktree?, branch?, title?, archived? }
Branches are genesis/<key> for a worktree session, or the repo's current branch when the session runs at the root. The design had invented run/<key>; that is now corrected everywhere it appeared.
noWorktree is a posture, not a constant. It is a workspace default that a session binds stickily on its first turn, so “worktree per run” is true of some sessions and false of others — a nested monorepo runs at the root by design.
confined is the real security flag and walkie's screens now surface it. True means the spawn drops every inherited MCP server; false means the session carries the operator's MCP servers, Gmail, Drive and Calendar connectors. MCP runs outside the filesystem sandbox, so nothing about path confinement touches it.
WHAT WALKIE ADDS THAT GENESIS DOES NOT HAVE
The voice reachability allowlist. The gate and the approve verb. Standing routines and their cadence. The ask log as an append-only per-user store with acknowledgement. Containment proof for voice approval. The orchestrator plane. None of these exist in Genesis today — every one is a thing to build, and the screens that show them are specifications rather than integrations.
There is already a voice channel in Genesis (apps/api/src/voice.ts, BRO-2228) but it is a different product: an ElevenLabs phone agent with voice for intake and WhatsApp for delivery. Its principle is worth inheriting though, and it is the same one the runtime board argues for — nothing in that handler runs an agent; every path answers from state already held or enqueues and returns.
